citation: Alexandre Varela, “Des peintures murales syriaques inédites: l’église Mor-Stephanos de Kfarbe dans le Ṭūr ‘Abdīn (Sud-est de la Turquie),” Convivium 8:2 (2021): 110–31.

data.title: Des peintures murales syriaques inédites: l’église Mor-Stephanos de Kfarbe dans le Ṭūr ‘Abdīn (Sud-est de la Turquie)
data.abstractNote: In southeastern Turkey, Tūr ʿAbdīn is an essential region for Syriac Christianity owing to its many churches and monasteries and to its religious importance during Middle Ages. Nevertheless, despite literary evidence of a figural painting tradition in Syriac church, most of the churches in Tūr ʿAbdīn have today no surviving painted decoration because of the ravages of time and long neglect. This paper offers a depiction and analysis of what seems to be the only monumental painting surviving in the region: the apse decoration of Mor-Stephanos Church in the village of Kfarbe. Recently discovered, these paintings warrant analysis of their iconography and stylistic interpretation. Using written sources and examples of Syriac figurative paintings outside Tūr ʿAbdīn, this article offers a hypothesis about the dating, style, and iconography of such an important testimony for Syriac art history.

data.title: Les constructions érémitiques dans le Ṭūr ‘Abdīn et la figure de Mor Barṣawmo: architecture et phénomène cultuel
data.abstractNote: In today’s Southeastern Turkey, the Ṭur ʿAbdīn region is one of the most important places for Syriac Christianity. Among the numerous churches and monasteries in this area, several buildings are dedicated to Mor Barṣawmo, an ascetic saint from the fifth century. This paper analyses how this figure became the patron saint of some churches dedicated to ascetic and eremitic religious practices. The second part of the paper includes a catalogue of churches and monasteries dedicated to Mor Barṣawmo and compares the material characteristics they share to establish a map of a cult phenomenon that seems to appear after the twelfth century in the region.

data.abstractNote: This article retraces the search for a painter, and tries to discover his identity. Some of his works were found in the Mosul region (Iraq). There he painted some saints for several Chaldean churches. However, his place of origin seems to be in the region around Mardin (Turkey). Probably he was an Armenian self-made artist who offered his services to different groups of Christians and expressed some characteristics of their spiritual identity in those lands during the XIX century. However, much more field research has to be done before reaching definitive results.

data.title: Marī en Kokhè
data.abstractNote:
P. Haddad, Bagdad, recently re-discovered the initial part of the so-called Chronicle of Si'irt (ed. by A. Scher in Patrologia Orientalis). According to this initial part the real name of the chronicle should be ‘Compiled Ecclesiastical History’. A fragment dealing with the history of Marī, his origins and his evangelization of al-Madā'in (Seleucia-Ctesiphon), the capital of the Persian Empire, is translated here for the first time in full.
The author compares his text with the legendary Vita Maris from the fifth century and the presumed reworking of Ch. 5 of the Kitāb el-Maǧdal by Marī bin Suleyma?n. It appears that Marī? bin Suleyma?n closely follows the ‘Compiled Ecclesiastical History’ rather than basing himself on the Kitāb el-Maǧdal. The article concludes with some information about the present state of the archaeological site of Kokhè (Seleucia).

data.abstractNote: In the footsteps of Fr J.-M. Fiey and under his guidance, the author of this article was able to pay a short visit to Northern Iraq, searching for architectural remains of ancient monasteries. citation: Robert E. van Voorst, “‘The Ascents of James’: History and Theology of a Jewish-Christian Community as Reflected in the Pseudo-Clementine ‘Recognitions’ 1:33-71” (Ph.D. dissertation, Union Theological Seminary, New York, 1988).

data.title: ‘The Ascents of James’: History and Theology of a Jewish-Christian Community as Reflected in the Pseudo-Clementine ‘Recognitions’ 1:33-71
data.abstractNote: Chapter One is a history of research into R 1.33-71. Research into the Recognitions (R) began around 1500. With the Tubingen School, R was considered important for understanding the New Testament Church. In 1849, R. Kostlin first isolated a source in R 1 and identified it as The Ascents of James (AJ; Greek Anabathmoi Iakobou known by the citation from Epiphanius’ Panarion. In the twentieth century, the hypothesis of an AJ source gained acceptance by most researchers, although the limits of the AJ in R 1 have been continually debated. Chapter Two uses source-critical methods to isolate a discrete document in R 1.33.3-1.44.3, 1.55-1.62, 1.64.1- 1.69.1, and 1.69.8-1.71. This source is then identified as The Ascents of James. The unity of the AJ is defended against H. J. Schoeps, G. Ludemann, and others. Chapter Three presents, in parallel columns, fresh translations of the AJ from the best critical texts of the Latin and Syriac versions of R 1. Chapter Four is a commentary on the AJ. It offers a treatment of technical matters (text, grammar, literary forms, etc.) and an interpretation of the three sections of the AJ: a history of salvation from Abraham to the early church (1.33-44); the debate of the Twelve Apostles with the Jewish parties in the temple (1.55-65); and the speech of James and its aftermath (1.66-71). Chapter Five analyzes the major issues of the interpretation of the AJ. The theology of the AJ centers on Jesus as the Mosaic Prophet and Messiah. The historicity of the AJ’s portrait of the earliest church is rejected. In its imaginative narrative, however the AJ community presents its own belief. This community is a Jewish-Christian church in the area of Pella in Transjordan. It observes the Mosaic law and practices baptism as the replacement of sacrifice. It blames Paul for preventing the success of the mission to the Jews. The AJ was written in the second half of the second century to reinforce the faith and self-understanding of its community.

data.title: The Syro-Hexaplaric Headings of the Psalms in Manuscript 12t3
data.abstractNote: he Syriac manuscript 12t3 contains many unique variant readings in the headings of the Psalms. This manuscript contains the text of the Psalms according to the Peshitta, but has variants from the Syro-Hexapla added between the lines. It has the headings of the Syro-Hexapla, in full, not between the lines as is the case for the Psalms themselves. This paper considers the headings in this manuscript on their own, as the headings can in some cases reflect a different tradition from that contained in the Psalms themselves. A survey of the variants in the headings of the Psalms in different manuscripts of the Syro-Hexapla is presented followed by a detailed discussion of the headings in manuscript 12t3. This manuscript contains quite a number of unique variants. Some of the variants show hexaplaric influence, others agree with Aquila and Symmachus and influence from other Syriac traditions of  the headings to the Psalms can also be found.

data.title: The Headings of the Psalms in the East Syriac Tradition Reconsidered
data.abstractNote: In the first half of the previous century the headings of the Psalms in the East Syriac tradition received a lot of attention, with important contributions by scholars such as Devreesse and Vosté. In 1960 Bloemendaal published an edition of these headings. Since 1960 a number of important new manuscripts became available, as well as a translation of the commentary of Theodore and a translation of the commentary of Diodore on the first fifty Psalms. This paper deals with the light shed on the history of the East Syrian headings particularly by two manuscripts not available to Bloemendaal. The examples discussed lead one to the conclusion that 6t1, used by Bloemendaal, must not be regarded as the paradigmatic witness in all instances.
